subject: Blended slab true-up: rounding and long-context treatment for bursty workloads

Subject: True-up and slab question for upcoming renewal

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. As we start the renewal prep, procurement asked for a short written explanation on how Redwood will account for our ‘burst-heavy’ usage pattern under the proposed blended slab. Two quick points they flagged:

- When we have short microbursts (2–5 minute spikes) across many users, how are those rounded for slab true-ups? Do you aggregate per-call or per-conversation?
- For long-context flows (we sometimes send 8–12k token prompts in a single request), do those count as a single slab consumption or are they split into sub-units? If split, what rounding applies?

I attached a sample one-week usage extract (Acme_sample_usage_June.xlsx). Could you provide an example invoice calculation or a short worked example showing the rounding and minimums?

Procurement is also interested in whether any pilot concession on minimums is reasonable for a 12-month renewal.

Appreciate a concise write-up we can share with legal and finance.

Subject: Re: True-up and slab question for upcoming renewal — worked example + rules

Elaine / Kimberly / Jordan — below is a concise synopsis of how the proposed blended-slab true-up will treat Acme’s usage pattern, plus a small numeric example based on the attached sample. I tried to keep this procurement-friendly but technically accurate.

Summary of rules (short):
- Unit definition: billing is measured in "billing-units" where 1 billing-unit = 1,000 tokens.
- Per-call accounting: each request is accounted independently at the call boundary unless it is part of an explicit streaming session.
- Aggregation window: for true-up and amortization we aggregate all billing-units within the invoice period; there is no cross-invoice carry-forward except for credited pilot concessions.
- Rounding: each call consumption is first converted to billing-units (ceil to next whole unit at the call level). After that, invoice-line aggregation sums units and applies slab pricing.
- Minimums: there is a per-call minimum floor of 1 billing-unit (i.e., calls <1k tokens round up to 1k); there is no artificial per-conversation minimum unless requested in the contract.
- Long-context split: single requests that exceed 16k tokens are split into 16k windowed segments on the runtime and invoiced as the sum of those segments (each segment is ceil'd to billing-units). For Acme’s common 8–12k calls, they remain a single call and are ceil'd once.
- Microburst behavior: short microbursts produce many small calls; because rounding is at call-level, microbursts will incur more ceil-rounding loss than long, amortized calls. Example concession options below.

Worked example (based on sheet):
- Week sample: 1,240 calls over 7 days. Breakdown: 940 calls between 200–900 tokens; 260 calls at 8,000–11,500 tokens.
- Call-level conversion:
  * Small calls (940 calls): average 600 tokens -> ceil(0.6k) = 1 billing-unit each => 940 units
  * Large calls (260 calls): average 9.5k tokens -> ceil(9.5k / 1k) = 10 billing-units each => 2,600 units
  * Total units (week): 3,540 billing-units

If the contractual slab has bands (e.g., Tier A: 0–10k units @ $0.025/unit, Tier B: 10k–50k @ $0.020/unit), the weekly total would be prorated to the invoice period and priced according to the slab. Rounding for the slab happens after call-level ceil — we do not additionally round the aggregate to a larger quantum.

Concession options for procurement to reduce microburst rounding pain:
- Pilot smoothing credit: apply a pilot smoothing credit that refunds the first 5% of units above measured baseline for three months.
- Call-batching suggestion: if you can buffer microbursts into client-side batching (even 2x batching), you reduce ceil overhead by ~40–50%.
- Minimum redefinition: convert the per-call floor to a per-session floor for a defined session boundary (e.g., intra-client 2-minute window) — requires instrumentation to assert session boundaries.

Edge case: streaming sessions
- For explicit streaming sessions (client uses streaming API and appends tokens across a connection), we amortize token accounting over the streaming session and ceil at the session boundary instead of per-frame. That reduces rounding for multi-frame streams.

Next steps from our side:
- Kimberly / Jordan: propose one of the concession options and approximate commercial impact for the 12-month renewal.
- Kimberly: we’ll produce a concise one-page summary (procurement-ready) and a short sample invoice line replacing weekly sample with monthly projection.
